title: Elevator system
scopeHtml:
Scope: requirements, SCAN stop handling, cost-based dispatcher, runnable Java and Kotlin, locking and lock ordering, follow-ups.

Scope: requirements, SCAN stop handling, cost-based dispatcher, runnable Java and Kotlin, locking and lock ordering, follow-ups.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design the control logic for a building with several elevators. Two kinds of requests exist: a hall call (button outside: floor and direction) and a car call (button inside: destination floor).

Functional:

  • N elevators, F floors. A hall call must be assigned to one elevator.
  • Each elevator serves its stops without reversing needlessly (people hate that).
  • An idle elevator waits where it is; a moving elevator keeps its direction while stops remain ahead.

Non-functional: the assignment rule must be replaceable; the elevator must be a testable object with no real clock (we drive it with step()).

Out of scope: door timing, weight limits, express zones, emergency mode (Follow-ups).

Worked example. One elevator at floor 0 gets stops 5, 2, 8. It goes up and serves 2, 5, 8 in order (not 5, 2, 8). Total travel 8 floors. A naive first-come order would travel 5 + 3 + 6 = 14 floors. That saving is why SCAN exists.

Industry examples. This is the disk "elevator algorithm" (SCAN/LOOK) that Linux I/O schedulers used for spinning disks. Real buildings (Otis, Schindler) use destination dispatch: you press the target floor in the lobby and the group controller assigns a car.

Everyday analogy. A bus on a one-way loop picking up everyone along the route before turning back.

Common interview traps.

  • Serving requests first come first served; it zigzags.
  • Treating hall calls and car calls as the same thing (a hall call has a direction people want).

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Direction: UP, DOWN, IDLE.
  • Elevator: current floor, direction, a sorted set of stops (TreeSet), a log of served floors, step().
  • Dispatcher: owns all elevators; call(floor, direction) picks the cheapest one with a cost function.
  • Request: just an int stop, because the sorted set removes the need for a request class at this size.

Why a TreeSet. higher(floor) and lower(floor) answer "is there anything ahead?" in O(log n), and de-duplicates presses of the same button.

Decision gravity. The cost function (distance, plus a penalty for going the wrong way or for a long queue) is the heart and is easy to change later. Making the dispatcher pick at call time ("greedy assignment") is simple; the alternative is to re-balance on every tick, which is smarter but harder to explain and test. Reversible.

Everyday analogy. The set of stops is a to-do list sorted by floor; the elevator always continues the same way until the list ahead is empty.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a queue for stops; the order of requests is not the order of service.
  • Letting Dispatcher reach inside the elevator's fields.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
+----------------------+   has many   +------------------------+
 | Dispatcher           |------------->| Elevator               |
 |  cars: List<Elevator>|              |  id, floor, dir        |
 |  call(floor, dir)    |  uses cost() |  stops: TreeSet<Int>   |
 +----------------------+              |  served: List<Int>     |
                                       |  addStop(f), step()    |
                                       |  idle(), cost(f, d)    |
                                       +-----------^------------+
                                                   |
                                         SafeElevator (synchronized)
 enum Direction { UP, DOWN, IDLE }
 SafeDispatcher extends Dispatcher (synchronized call)

 Elevator state machine:  IDLE --addStop--> UP/DOWN --stops empty--> IDLE

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting that the elevator itself is a small state machine (IDLE, UP, DOWN).
  • Putting the cost logic in the dispatcher, where it needs the elevator's private data.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Strategy (assignment rule). The cost comparison can become a DispatchStrategy interface: nearest car, least loaded, zone-based. Alternative: hard-code nearest. Cheap to introduce when asked.
  • State (elevator direction). IDLE/UP/DOWN could be State objects as in the vending machine. Here an enum plus the SCAN rule in step() is shorter; say you would refactor if door and maintenance states appear.
  • Observer (optional). Floor displays subscribe to elevator position events instead of polling.
  • Command (optional). Each request as an object makes logging and undo easier.

Industry examples. Kubernetes schedulers also use a "cost/score" function to place pods, the same idea as cost(). Uber dispatch assigns the nearest driver with penalties, a comparable greedy-with-penalty design.

Everyday analogy. A school bus: it keeps going forward picking up kids, turns around only at the end of the route.

Common interview traps.

  • Reaching for State pattern with 8 classes before the logic is correct.
  • No story for starvation: a far floor can wait forever if new nearer calls keep arriving (mention an aging bonus).

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Java (compiled and run with JDK 21):

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

enum Direction { UP, DOWN, IDLE }

class Elevator {
    final int id;
    protected int floor = 0;
    protected Direction dir = Direction.IDLE;
    protected final TreeSet<Integer> stops = new TreeSet<>();
    final List<Integer> served = new ArrayList<>();   // floors where the doors opened

    Elevator(int id) { this.id = id; }

    void addStop(int f) { if (f != floor) stops.add(f); else served.add(f); }

    /** One tick = move one floor. SCAN: keep going the same way while stops remain ahead. */
    void step() {
        if (stops.isEmpty()) { dir = Direction.IDLE; return; }
        boolean above = stops.higher(floor) != null, below = stops.lower(floor) != null;
        if (dir == Direction.UP && !above) dir = Direction.DOWN;
        else if (dir == Direction.DOWN && !below) dir = Direction.UP;
        else if (dir == Direction.IDLE) dir = above ? Direction.UP : Direction.DOWN;
        floor += dir == Direction.UP ? 1 : -1;
        if (stops.remove(floor)) served.add(floor);
        if (stops.isEmpty()) dir = Direction.IDLE;
    }

    boolean idle() { return stops.isEmpty(); }

    /** Lower is better. Heading our way and not yet passed = cheap. */
    int cost(int f, Direction want) {
        int dist = Math.abs(floor - f);
        if (dir == Direction.IDLE) return dist;
        boolean onTheWay = (dir == Direction.UP && f >= floor && want != Direction.DOWN)
                        || (dir == Direction.DOWN && f <= floor && want != Direction.UP);
        return onTheWay ? dist : dist + 20 + stops.size();   // 20 ~ a full trip penalty, tune it
    }
}

class Dispatcher {
    protected final List<? extends Elevator> cars;
    Dispatcher(List<? extends Elevator> cars) { this.cars = cars; }

    /** Hall call: someone on `floor` pressed UP or DOWN. */
    Elevator call(int floor, Direction want) {
        Elevator best = cars.get(0);
        for (Elevator e : cars) if (e.cost(floor, want) < best.cost(floor, want)) best = e;
        best.addStop(floor);
        return best;
    }
}

Kotlin core of one elevator and the dispatcher (hand translated, not compiled in this session):

enum class Direction { UP, DOWN, IDLE }

class Elevator(val id: Int) {
    var floor = 0
    var dir = Direction.IDLE
    private val stops = java.util.TreeSet<Int>()
    val served = mutableListOf<Int>()

    @Synchronized fun addStop(f: Int) { if (f != floor) stops.add(f) else served += f }
    @Synchronized fun idle() = stops.isEmpty()

    @Synchronized fun step() {
        if (stops.isEmpty()) { dir = Direction.IDLE; return }
        val above = stops.higher(floor) != null
        val below = stops.lower(floor) != null
        if (dir == Direction.UP && !above) dir = Direction.DOWN
        else if (dir == Direction.DOWN && !below) dir = Direction.UP
        else if (dir == Direction.IDLE) dir = if (above) Direction.UP else Direction.DOWN
        floor += if (dir == Direction.UP) 1 else -1
        if (stops.remove(floor)) served += floor
        if (stops.isEmpty()) dir = Direction.IDLE
    }

    @Synchronized fun cost(f: Int, want: Direction): Int {
        val dist = kotlin.math.abs(floor - f)
        if (dir == Direction.IDLE) return dist
        val onTheWay = (dir == Direction.UP && f >= floor && want != Direction.DOWN) ||
                       (dir == Direction.DOWN && f <= floor && want != Direction.UP)
        return if (onTheWay) dist else dist + 20 + stops.size
    }
}

class Dispatcher(private val cars: List<Elevator>) {
    @Synchronized fun call(floor: Int, want: Direction): Elevator =
        cars.minByOrNull { it.cost(floor, want) }!!.also { it.addStop(floor) }
}

Common interview traps.

  • Moving two floors in a tick or skipping the stop at the arrival floor.
  • Forgetting the "already here" case in addStop (opens the doors immediately).

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Elevator e = new Elevator(1);
        e.addStop(5); e.addStop(2); e.addStop(8);
        while (!e.idle()) e.step();
        System.out.println("order = " + e.served);            // [2, 5, 8]

        e.addStop(6);                                          // at 8 now, going down for 6
        while (!e.idle()) e.step();
        System.out.println("then = " + e.served);              // [2, 5, 8, 6]

        Elevator a = new Elevator(1), b = new Elevator(2);
        b.floor = 9;
        System.out.println("floor 2 call goes to car " + new Dispatcher(List.of(a, b)).call(2, Direction.UP).id); // 1

        List<SafeElevator> cars = List.of(new SafeElevator(1), new SafeElevator(2), new SafeElevator(3));
        SafeDispatcher d = new SafeDispatcher(cars);
        ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
        List<Future<?>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int f = 1; f <= 30; f++) { final int fl = f; fs.add(ex.submit(() -> d.call(fl, Direction.UP))); }
        for (Future<?> fu : fs) fu.get();
        ex.shutdown();
        int guard = 0;
        while (cars.stream().anyMatch(c -> !c.idle()) && guard++ < 1000) cars.forEach(SafeElevator::step);
        Set<Integer> all = new TreeSet<>();
        for (SafeElevator c : cars) all.addAll(c.served);
        System.out.println("floors served = " + all.size());   // 30
    }
}

Actual output from javac Demo.java && java Demo:

order = [2, 5, 8]
then = [2, 5, 8, 6]
floor 2 call goes to car 1
floors served = 30

The last line proves 30 concurrent hall calls to 3 cars all get served exactly once somewhere.

Common interview traps.

  • Tests that sleep in real time; the tick-driven step() keeps tests instant.
  • Not testing direction reversal (the 8 then 6 case).

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
Many threads touch an elevator: passengers pressing buttons (any thread), the motor loop calling step() every second, and the dispatcher reading cost(). TreeSet is not thread-safe; a button press during higher() can corrupt the structure or throw ConcurrentModificationException.

Fix and gravity. Make each elevator a monitor (synchronized methods): operations are tiny, so contention is negligible. The dispatcher also needs one lock so "read all costs, choose, add stop" is atomic; otherwise two simultaneous calls compute against the same stale costs and both pick the same car.

class SafeElevator extends Elevator {
    SafeElevator(int id) { super(id); }
    @Override synchronized void addStop(int f) { super.addStop(f); }
    @Override synchronized void step() { super.step(); }
    @Override synchronized boolean idle() { return super.idle(); }
    @Override synchronized int cost(int f, Direction w) { return super.cost(f, w); }
}

class SafeDispatcher extends Dispatcher {
    SafeDispatcher(List<SafeElevator> cars) { super(cars); }
    // choose + assign must be one atomic step, or two calls pick the same car using stale costs
    @Override synchronized Elevator call(int floor, Direction want) { return super.call(floor, want); }
}

Alternative. A single-threaded event loop per elevator with a BlockingQueue of commands: no locks, easy to reason about, and the natural shape in real controllers (Kafka-style "one writer per partition"). It is a bigger rewrite; choose it when the logic grows.

Lock ordering. SafeDispatcher.call holds the dispatcher lock and then takes each elevator lock. Never call the dispatcher while holding an elevator lock, or you get deadlock.

Symptom in production. A request vanishes (lost update on the set) or one car gets all the calls (stale costs). Metrics: calls assigned per car, p99 wait time.

Everyday analogy. Several people writing on one shared whiteboard: only one marker at a time, and the person deciding who goes where must stop everyone while checking the board.

Common interview traps.

  • Locking only the elevator but not the choose-and-assign step in the dispatcher.
  • Calling out to a slow display or log while holding the lock.
  • Using Collections.synchronizedSortedSet and then iterating without holding its lock.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Destination dispatch. Passenger enters target floor in the lobby; the dispatcher groups people going the same way. Replace the cost function.
  • Capacity. Track load; skip hall calls for a full car.
  • Express/zone elevators. A strategy restricts which floors a car may serve.
  • Starvation. Add an age bonus to old requests inside cost.
  • Maintenance/emergency. New elevator state OUT_OF_SERVICE; dispatcher skips it; fire mode sends all cars to the ground floor.
  • Peak traffic. Park idle cars at the lobby in the morning, at the top floors in the evening.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering every follow-up by adding flags to Elevator; name which class or interface should grow.
  • Ignoring that 1 elevator versus 6 elevators changes the problem (assignment matters).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Two request kinds: hall calls (floor and direction) and car calls (target floor).
  • Each elevator keeps a sorted set of stops and uses the SCAN rule: continue in the same direction while stops lie ahead, then reverse.
  • The dispatcher assigns each hall call to the elevator with the lowest cost (distance plus penalties); strategy-ready.
  • Concurrency: guard the stop set with the elevator's monitor and make "choose and assign" atomic in the dispatcher; keep lock order dispatcher, then elevator.
  • Extensions: destination dispatch, capacity, zones, starvation aging, out-of-service state.

questions.promptHtml: Why does an elevator keep its stops in a sorted set and continue in one direction instead of serving requests first come first served?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks you know the SCAN/LOOK idea and can justify the data structure.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: FCFS zigzags: with stops 5, 2, 8 from floor 0 it travels 5 + 3 + 6 = 14 floors; SCAN goes up serving 2, 5, 8 and travels 8. A TreeSet gives higher(floor) and lower(floor) in O(log n) to answer "is anything ahead?", and de-duplicates repeated button presses. The elevator keeps its direction while stops remain ahead, then reverses.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
IDLE --addStop--> UP/DOWN --stops empty--> IDLE
step(): if direction UP and nothing above -> DOWN; if DOWN and nothing below -> UP;
        move one floor; if floor in stops -> remove + open doors

This is the disk elevator algorithm. A queue is wrong because request order is not service order. A request is just an int floor here, so no request class is needed at this size.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a queue or list for stops.
  • Skipping the "already on this floor" case in addStop (open the doors immediately).
  • Moving two floors per tick.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the cost of higher on a TreeSet? -> O(log n); n is tiny, so clarity matters more.
  2. Can this starve a floor? -> Yes, if nearer calls keep arriving; add an age bonus.
  3. Why is a hall call different from a car call? -> Hall call carries the wanted direction; car call is only a target floor.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "sort the requests". Senior: states the travel numbers, the O(log n) lookups, the reversal rule and the starvation risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Group controllers use the same idea; naive FCFS controllers were the cause of "the lift ignores me" complaints.

questions.promptHtml: How does the dispatcher choose which elevator serves a hall call, and which pattern would you extract from it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The assignment rule is the heart of the problem; they want a justified rule and a replaceable one.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each elevator returns a cost for a (floor, direction) request: distance, plus a penalty when it is heading the wrong way or has a long queue. The dispatcher picks the lowest cost and adds the stop. I extract a DispatchStrategy (nearest, least loaded, zone based) so the rule is replaceable. It is greedy at call time, which is simple and testable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
int cost(int f, Direction want) {
    int dist = Math.abs(floor - f);
    if (dir == Direction.IDLE) return dist;
    boolean onTheWay = (dir == UP && f >= floor && want != DOWN) || (dir == DOWN && f <= floor && want != UP);
    return onTheWay ? dist : dist + 20 + stops.size();
}

Alternative: re-balance every tick, which is smarter but harder to explain and test. The elevator itself is a small state machine (IDLE, UP, DOWN); an enum is fine now, State objects if door and maintenance states appear.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting the cost logic in the dispatcher where it needs the elevator's private data.
  • A fixed penalty constant that does not scale with the building height.
  • No starvation story.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Who owns cost? -> The elevator, since it knows its own state.
  2. Where would Observer fit? -> Floor displays subscribe to position events.
  3. How do you evaluate a cost function? -> Simulate a day of traffic and compare average and p99 wait.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "closest elevator". Senior: direction-aware cost, strategy extraction, greedy versus rebalancing trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Kubernetes-style scoring and ride dispatch use the same greedy-with-penalty design.

questions.contextHtml:
With 3 cars, a morning rush produced these assignment metrics: car 1 got 91 percent of hall calls in 5 minutes, p99 wait went from 22 s to 80 s. Code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

    Elevator call(int floor, Direction want) {          // no lock
        Elevator best = cars.get(0);
        for (Elevator e : cars) if (e.cost(floor, want) < best.cost(floor, want)) best = e;
        best.addStop(floor);                            // elevator methods are synchronized
        return best;
    }
}
class Dispatcher(private val cars: List<Elevator>) {

        cars.minByOrNull { it.cost(floor, want) }!!.also { it.addStop(floor) }   // Elevator methods @Synchronized
}
questions.promptHtml: Why does one car get all the calls even though every elevator method is synchronized?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Elevator is already synchronized, so it is safe" and blames the cost function.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many calls arrive within one tick? Is the load metric stops.size() read under the elevator lock? Is step() on its own thread?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make call synchronized on the dispatcher so choose and assign is one step.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Many simultaneous calls compute costs against the same stale state, all choose the same best car before any assignment lands. Second: the cost function ties break to index 0 (cars.get(0) first), amplifying the effect. Third: the penalty is too small so one car always looks cheapest.
  4. How I'd verify each: A test firing 30 calls from 8 threads and asserting calls per car are spread; log the cost vector per assignment.
  5. Root cause: Per-object atomicity does not give atomicity of the compound operation read-all-costs, choose, add stop.
  6. Fix: A lock in the dispatcher around the compound step, with lock order dispatcher then elevator and never the reverse. Tie-break on fewest stops.
  7. Prevention: Metric of calls per car and p99 wait; the concurrent assignment test in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A dispatcher lock is cheap (microseconds per call). I would not take a lock per elevator and hold all of them; one dispatcher lock is enough. An event loop with a single writer is the bigger-rewrite alternative.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Could ConcurrentModificationException still appear? -> Not in TreeSet if every access goes through the elevator's synchronized methods.
  • What if call logs to a slow service? -> Do it after releasing the lock.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A building controller sent 14 calls to one car in the same 50 ms because the cost read and the stop write were separate steps; the fix was one method-level lock.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the cost function only.
  • Hire: identifies the compound operation and locks it.
  • Strong hire: states lock order, tie-breaker, and the single-writer alternative.

questions.contextHtml:
In a 40-floor tower, complaints: "a person on floor 38 waited 6 minutes". Data for one car:

t=0    car at 5 going UP, stops {7, 9, 12, 38}
t=20s  new hall calls 8, 10, 11, 13 appended nearer the car
t=60s  new hall calls 14, 15, 16 ...  (arrivals every 10 s on floors 6 to 20)
car keeps serving nearer floors; 38 stays in the set

Average wait is 28 s (fine); p99 is 6 min.
questions.promptHtml: What is the problem, and how do you fix it without wrecking the average?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use FCFS" or "add more elevators".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the goal average wait or a worst-case bound? Are all 3 cars busy? Is a hall call assigned once or reassigned?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap the wait: a request older than 90 s gets a large cost discount so the dispatcher routes it to a car that can take it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Starvation of far requests under the greedy nearest rule. Second: the car never reverses because new stops always appear ahead. Red herring: average wait is fine, so a mean-based alert would never fire.
  4. How I'd verify each: Track per-request age and alert on p99; replay the traffic in a simulation.
  5. Root cause: SCAN plus continuous nearer arrivals; no aging.
  6. Fix: Add an age term in cost: cost - age_seconds / 5 (floor at 0 when old, tune with simulation), and let a car that has an old request ahead stop accepting new hall calls in the current sweep. Reversal still at the end of the sweep.
  7. Prevention: Per-request latency histogram, p99 alerts, simulation test with adversarial arrivals.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Aging worsens the average slightly; I accept that for a bounded worst case. I would not drop SCAN: FCFS travels roughly twice as far in the notes' example.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just a second queue for old requests? -> Equivalent, but an aged cost keeps one scoring function and one place to tune.
  • Does this also protect the stop inside a car? -> A car call is already committed in the car's set; the sweep ends when nothing remains ahead.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A building's mean wait looked great for months; only a complaint about the top floor revealed a 5-minute tail.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: FCFS or more cars.
  • Hire: aging in the cost, p99 monitoring.
  • Strong hire: sweep-end rule, simulation test, accepts the average-versus-tail trade-off.

questions.contextHtml: The client wants (1) destination dispatch (passengers type their target floor in the lobby), (2) express cars that serve only floors 30 to 40 and the lobby, and (3) a car that is full (load sensor) must skip hall calls.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change, which do not, and where do the new rules live?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds isExpress, isFull, destination flags to Elevator and ifs in call.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is destination dispatch for all floors or the lobby only? How do passengers learn which car? Is capacity by weight or by count?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; extend.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The cost function and an eligibility check are the only places that vary; the Elevator SCAN logic stays.
  4. How I'd verify each: Tests: express car never gets floor 12; a full car is never assigned a hall call; destination groups share a car.
  5. Root cause (design): a planned extension.
  6. Fix: DispatchStrategy interface with the current greedy as default; eligible(car, request) as part of the strategy for zones and capacity; a DestinationDispatch strategy that takes (from, to) and groups requests going the same way. Elevator gains load and a floor-range filter only if the car owns them; the dispatcher stays a thin loop over the strategy.
  7. Prevention: Strategy tests with fake elevators.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Destination dispatch changes the request type (from, to), so a small Request class now appears; I would not introduce it earlier.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Car capacity but a car call for a full car? -> The passenger is already inside; capacity affects hall call eligibility, not stops already queued.
  • Fire mode? -> New elevator state sending all cars to the ground floor; the dispatcher skips cars in that state.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Express zones were implemented as if (floor > 30) inside step(), then every maintenance mode needed to touch it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flags on Elevator.
  • Hire: strategy and eligibility, Elevator mostly unchanged.
  • Strong hire: introduces the request object only when needed and names what each change costs.

questions.contextHtml:
After adding floor display callbacks, the building control service freezes every few days. Thread dump excerpt:

"motor-loop-2"  BLOCKED on Dispatcher@3f2a   (holds SafeElevator@91c2)
    at SafeDispatcher.call(...)    at DisplayListener.onArrive(...)   at SafeElevator.step(...)
"http-call-17"  BLOCKED on SafeElevator@91c2 (holds Dispatcher@3f2a)
    at SafeElevator.addStop(...)    at SafeDispatcher.call(...)
Found one Java-level deadlock
questions.promptHtml: Explain the deadlock and fix it. What rule do you enforce?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use tryLock with a timeout everywhere" without finding the cycle, or removing locks.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does onArrive do (it re-dispatches?)? Is it synchronous inside step()? How often does it fire?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart the service; disable the display callback re-dispatch behind a flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Lock order inversion: call takes dispatcher then elevator; step holds the elevator lock and the callback calls the dispatcher (elevator then dispatcher). Second: a long callback holding a lock. Third: nested calls on a non-reentrant lock.
  4. How I'd verify each: jstack shows the cycle (above); search code for calls out of synchronized regions.
  5. Root cause: Calling an external callback while holding an elevator lock, which can call back into the dispatcher.
  6. Fix: Enforce the order dispatcher then elevator everywhere, and never call out while holding either lock: inside step() collect events (arrived floor) into a local list, release the lock, then notify listeners. Or post events to a queue handled by another thread.
  7. Prevention: A code review rule: no alien calls under a lock; a test with a listener that calls the dispatcher.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a timed tryLock to hide the inversion (it hides the bug). The single-thread-per-elevator event loop removes most lock reasoning but is a larger rewrite.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why do "synchronized" calls on a Collections.synchronizedSortedSet not help? -> Iteration still needs the set's lock held by the caller.
  • How do you detect this in staging? -> Run the stress test with a re-entrant listener and enable deadlock detection (ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A notification callback inside a lock caused a freeze once per week at the same hour; the cycle only appeared when two events overlapped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random timeouts.
  • Hire: identifies the inversion and moves callbacks outside the lock.
  • Strong hire: states the global lock-order rule, adds a detection test, offers the event-loop alternative.

questions.contextHtml:
A tower has 80 floors and 24 cars in 4 banks. Morning rush: 1,200 hall calls per minute, mostly from the lobby going up. The cost uses dist + 20 + stops.size() for a car going the wrong way. Simulation shows many cars bunched near the lobby and p99 wait of 95 s.

Example: car A at floor 10 going UP with 6 stops; a hall call DOWN at floor 5. Car B is idle at floor 70.
questions.promptHtml: Compute the costs for A and B, say what is wrong, and propose a better scoring design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase 20 to 100" without a model of why.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the objective (average wait, p99, energy)? Do we know destinations? Is this bank-limited?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Scale the penalty to the building (about 2 x floors) and re-run the simulation.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: For A: not on the way (UP, call is below and wants DOWN), so cost = 5 + 20 + 6 = 31. For B (idle): 65. So A wins, though A must finish 6 stops going up first, maybe 70 floors of travel, while B is far but free. The constant 20 is tuned for small buildings. Second: all idle cars stay at their last floor, so none waits near the lobby for the rush.
  4. How I'd verify each: Offline simulation with recorded traffic; compare p99 and average per scoring variant.
  5. Root cause: A distance-only proxy for time; ignores the remaining work of a car.
  6. Fix: Estimate time-to-serve: remaining travel to finish the current sweep, plus the trip back to the call, plus about a fixed time per stop (doors). Use estimated seconds as the cost. Add idle repositioning (park idle cars at the lobby in the morning, high floors in the evening) as a strategy, zone banks per floor range.
  7. Prevention: The simulator is a regression harness; changing the strategy requires a before/after run.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A time estimate is more complex and needs door/stop time numbers (verify with the vendor). I would not move to full re-balancing every tick before the greedy estimate is measured.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• With destination dispatch, what changes? -> Group riders with similar destinations; the cost includes the number of stops added to the car.
  • How do you compare strategies fairly? -> Same recorded arrival trace, fixed seeds, report mean and p99.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A constant tuned on a 6-floor test building was shipped unchanged to a 60-floor one and produced bunching.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: arbitrary constant change.
  • Hire: computes 31 vs 65, explains why wrong, estimates time.
  • Strong hire: idle repositioning, zoned banks, simulation as a harness.

questions.contextHtml: Tests drive the elevator with Thread.sleep(1000) per floor and a background thread; the suite takes 14 minutes and fails 8 percent of the time. You must add tests for direction reversal (at 8 then a call at 6), idle behaviour, and the 30-calls-3-cars concurrency case.
questions.promptHtml: How do you design the tests and what do you assert?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Increase sleeps.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is time injected or does the elevator own a thread? Is step() public?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drive with while (!e.idle()) e.step(); no threads, no clock.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Real time and threads cause the flake; the tick-driven design exists to avoid them.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the suite 100 times, count failures.
  5. Root cause: The test harness depends on wall time.
  6. Fix: Deterministic tests: stops {5,2,8} from floor 0 gives served [2,5,8]; then a call at 6 from floor 8 gives [..., 8, 6] (reversal); a call at the current floor opens doors without moving; a duplicate stop is served once. Dispatcher test with fake elevators at known floors checks the chosen car. Concurrency: 8 threads send 30 hall calls to 3 cars, then step all cars in a loop with a guard of 1000 ticks, and assert the union of served floors has size 30 and each floor was served once.
  7. Prevention: No sleeps, a guard counter to avoid infinite loops in tests, a simulation test for starvation.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The union check does not prove balance; add a calls-per-car assertion with a tolerance. I would not mock TreeSet.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do you test lock order? -> A stress test with a re-entrant listener and a deadlock timeout in the test (fail if not complete in N seconds).
  • How do you test cost? -> Property tests: moving a car closer never increases its cost for a call on its way.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sleep-based elevator test suite was disabled by the team because of flakes; a real regression in reversal logic then shipped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: longer sleeps.
  • Hire: tick-driven tests including reversal and the concurrent union check.
  • Strong hire: guard counters, balance assertion, property tests and deadlock timeout.
